intro: An adverb describes an action. A comparative compares two actions. A superlative compares one action with a group of three or more.
scopeNote: Core rules match the experiments. Extra reading covers more textbook patterns.
sourceNote: Based on teacher-provided Chapter 6, pages 32–35. Examples have been rewritten.

sections.title: Compare actions: than and the
sections.text: Than connects the other action in a comparison. The usually comes before a superlative adverb, but it can be omitted in these examples.
examples: Ming runs faster than Tom.
Of three runners, Ming runs (the) fastest.
sections.note: Than can be omitted when the other action is understood. In Lab gaps, comparative answers must include than. Brackets show optional the.

sections.title: Short adverbs: endings and early
sections.text: Fast and hard add -er/-est. Late adds -r/-st. Early changes its final y: remove y, then add -ier/-iest. Choose ×y in both Lab forms.
examples: Mei arrived earlier than Jun.
Among three pupils, Jun worked hardest.

sections.title: Most -ly adverbs: more and most
sections.text: Adverbs ending in -ly usually use more/most. Keep the base unchanged. Early is an exception. Never add -er/-est directly to loudly, slowly or carefully.
examples: Mei writes more carefully than Jun.
Among three speakers, Jun spoke most clearly.

sections.title: Irregular forms: well, badly and far
sections.text: These adverbs change form. For distance, both farther/further and farthest/furthest are correct.
examples: Jun played better than before.
Of three walkers, Mei walked furthest.
sections.note: Use good for people or things; use well for how someone does something. More badly/most badly can also describe damage.

sections.title: Common mistakes: hard and hardly
sections.text: Use one comparison pattern, not two. Hard means with effort; hardly means almost not. They have different meanings.
examples: I worked hard on my homework.
I could hardly hear the teacher.

sections.title: Build the whole phrase
sections.text: Select ×y after early and before -ier/-iest; y never disappears automatically. The base is first in the available tray, not always first in your answer. Choose the or more first when needed.
recipes: more + carefully + than → more carefully than
sections.note: The is optional in these adverb superlatives: early + ×y + -iest also builds earliest.

sections.title: Less and least
sections.text: With longer adverbs, less compares two actions at a lower level. Least shows the lowest level in a group of three or more.
examples: Jun writes less carefully than Mei.
Of three pupils, Jun writes (the) least carefully.

sections.title: Stronger and softer comparisons
sections.text: Before a comparative, much, far and a lot make the difference stronger. A bit, a little and slightly make it softer.
examples: Mei runs much faster than Jun.
Jun arrived a little earlier than Mei.

sections.title: As and not as
sections.text: Use as + base adverb + as for equal actions. Use not as + base adverb + as for a lower level. With these verbs, put does not/do not before the base verb.
examples: Mei runs as fast as Tom.
Jun does not run as fast as Mei.

sections.title: Loud/loudly and slow/slowly
sections.text: These word families offer two patterns. Louder/loudest come from loud; slower/slowest come from slow. Loudly and slowly keep -ly and use more/most.
examples: Jun spoke louder / more loudly than before.
Mei walked slower / more slowly than Jun.
sections.note: In experiments, the bases loudly and slowly use more/most only. Do not turn slowly into slower.

sections.title: Matching comparisons and groups
sections.text: Compare how actions are done. Use of/among for a group and in for a place or group. I do can stand for I run.
examples: Ming runs faster than I do. (= I run)
Among her friends, Mei writes most carefully.
Of three runners, Ming runs fastest.
Mei works hardest in her class.
sections.note: Ming runs faster than me is also used in everyday English.

miniCheck.explanation: Clearly uses more clearly; than introduces the other action.

miniCheck.sentence: Of three teams, our blue team played _____.
miniCheck.explanation: Well changes to better/best. The best is correct; best is also natural here.
Early becomes earliest. In word blocks, choose early + ×y + -iest. The earliest and earliest are both natural here.
